passages.original: si vero Academiam veterem persequemur, quam nos ut scis probamus, quam erit illa acute explicanda nobis, quam argute quam obscure etiam contra Stoicos disserendum. Totum igitur illud philosophiae studium mihi quidem ipse sumo et ad vitae constantiam quantum possum et ad delectationem animi, nec ullum arbitror, ut apud Platonem est, maius aut melius a diis datum munus homini;
passages.english: But if we follow the Old Academy, which, as you know, I approve, how precisely we will have to explain it, how subtly, and even how obscurely we will have to argue against the Stoics! For my own part, then, I take up that whole pursuit of philosophy both for steadiness of life, as far as I can, and for the delight of the mind; nor do I think, as is said in Plato, that any greater or better gift has been given to man by the gods.
passages.notes: "quam obscure": some editors suspect the text here. The sense may be that the arguments are hard to follow, not that Cicero intends to argue obscurely.

passages.original: quid enim causae est cur poetas Latinos Graecis litteris eruditi legant, philosophos non legant? an quia delectat Ennius Pacuvius Accius multi alii, qui non verba sed vim Graecorum expresserunt poetarum—quanto magis philosophi delectabunt, si ut illi Aeschylum Sophoclem Euripidem sic hi Platonem imitentur Aristotelem Theophrastum. oratores quidem laudari video si qui e nostris Hyperidem sint aut Demosthenem imitati.
passages.english: For what reason is there why those educated in Greek literature should read the Latin poets but not read the [Latin] philosophers? Is it because Ennius, Pacuvius, Accius and many others give pleasure, who have rendered not the words but the force of the Greek poets? How much more will the philosophers give pleasure, if, as those [poets imitated] Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, so these imitate Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus! Orators at least, I see, are praised if any of our own have imitated Hyperides or Demosthenes.

passages.original: VA.Zeno igitur nullo modo is erat qui ut Theophrastus nervos virtutis inciderit, sed contra qui omnia quaeque ad beatam vitam pertinerent in una virtute poneret nec quicquam aliud numeraret in bonis idque appellaret honestum quod esset simplex quoddam et solum et unum bonum.
passages.english: Varro: Zeno, then, was by no means the man to cut the sinews of virtue, as Theophrastus did. On the contrary, he placed everything that pertained to the happy life in virtue alone, and counted nothing else among goods. He called that 'the honourable', which was a single, sole and unique good.
passages.notes: "VA." is taken as the speaker label for Varro.

passages.original: Tum ego Cum Zenone inquam ut accepimus Arcesilas sibi omne certamen instituit, non pertinacia aut studio vincendi ut quidem mihi videtur, sed earum rerum obscuritate, quae ad confessionem ignorationis adduxerant Socratem et vel ut iam ante Socratem Democritum Anaxagoram Empedoclem omnes paene veteres, qui nihil cognosci nihil percipi nihil sciri posse dixerunt, angustos sensus imbecillos animos brevia curricula vitae et ut Democritus in profundo veritatem esse demersam, opinionibus et institutis omnia teneri, nihil veritati relinqui, deinceps omnia tenebris circumfusa esse dixerunt.
passages.english: Then I said: It was with Zeno, as we have been told, that Arcesilas set up his whole contest. He did so not from obstinacy or eagerness to win, as it seems to me at least, but because of the obscurity of those matters which had brought Socrates to the admission of ignorance. Even before Socrates they had brought Democritus, Anaxagoras, Empedocles and almost all the ancients [to the same admission]. These said that nothing could be known, nothing perceived, nothing understood. They said that the senses are narrow, minds weak, and the courses of life short; and, as Democritus [said], that truth is sunk in the deep; that all things are held by opinions and conventions, and nothing is left to truth; and further, that all things are wrapped in darkness.
passages.notes: The construction "et vel ut iam ante Socratem" is awkward and may be corrupt; the sense given is the evident one. The sentence is repetitive ("dixerunt" twice) in the transmitted text.
